title: Threats: malware, phishing, social engineering
specPoints: Forms of attack: **malware** and **social engineering** (people as the weak point)
Types of malware — **virus**, **worm**, **trojan**, **spyware**, **ransomware** — what each does and how it spreads
learn: Define malware and name five types with what each one does
Describe how a virus, a worm and a trojan each spread differently
Define social engineering and explain why people are the weakest point in a system
Recognise phishing, blagging and shouldering in a scenario and name the method
Explain the impact of an attack on a person or an organisation
hook: Hold up your phone (screen off). Ask: how many messages this week asked you to 'click here', 'verify your account' or 'claim a prize'? Count hands. Now the surprise: most successful attacks on big companies did not break any code. Someone just asked nicely, and a person said yes. Today is about the attacks that target software, and the attacks that target you.

video.title: Malware and social engineering: attacking the machine and attacking the person
video.brief: 4 minutes. Split screen: a laptop on the left, a person on the right. Left side: five malware icons appear one by one — virus attaches to a file and copies when the file is opened; worm crawls across a network by itself; trojan is a gift box that opens to reveal malware; spyware is an eye watching keystrokes; ransomware padlocks the files and shows a ransom note. Right side: a phone buzzes with a fake bank text (phishing); a caller claims to be from IT and asks for a password (blagging); someone peers over a shoulder at a PIN (shouldering). Close with one line: software can be patched; people have to be trained.

explain.h: Two ways to attack a system
p: Every attack on a network goes through one of two doors. **Malware** attacks the machine: it is software written to damage, steal or take control. **Social engineering** attacks the person: it tricks a user into giving access, no code needed. The exam expects you to know both doors, name the methods, and say what each one does.

explain.h: Malware: five types you must know
p: Malware is short for 'malicious software'. The five named types differ in **what they do** and **how they spread**. Learn both halves for each.
explain.code:
Type        What it does                              How it spreads
----------  ----------------------------------------  ------------------------------------
Virus       Attaches to a file/program; damages or    Needs a user to open/run the
            corrupts data when run                    infected file; copies itself
Worm        Copies itself across a network; uses up   Spreads on its own through network
            bandwidth and memory, slows systems       connections — no user action needed
Trojan      Looks like useful software; once run it   User installs it on purpose,
            opens a 'back door' for the attacker      believing it is legitimate
Spyware     Secretly records activity — keystrokes,   Often bundled with other downloads
            passwords, screen — and sends it away     or dropped by a trojan
Ransomware  Encrypts the user's files and demands     Phishing attachments, infected
            payment for the key                       downloads, worms
after: Spotting the difference in the exam: a **virus needs a host file and a human to run it**; a **worm travels by itself**; a **trojan is invited in**. Those three contrasts are worth marks.

explain.h: Social engineering: the human weak point
p: **Social engineering** means manipulating people into breaking security rules or handing over information. It works because people want to be helpful, are in a hurry, or trust what looks official. A firewall cannot stop an employee reading out a password on the phone.
list: **Phishing**: a fake email, text or website pretending to be a trusted organisation (bank, school, delivery company) to get the user to enter login details or click a malicious link. Clues: urgency, odd sender address, spelling errors, links that do not match the text.

**Blagging (pretexting)**: the attacker invents a story to persuade the victim to hand over data or access — for example phoning reception as 'the new IT technician' and asking for the Wi-Fi password.
**Shouldering (shoulder surfing)**: watching someone type a PIN or password, directly or on camera, at a cash machine, a till or in a classroom.

p: Exam questions often ask for the **impact** of an attack on a business, school or hospital. Give specific consequences, not just 'it is bad'.
list: Loss or theft of **personal data** — customers, patients, students — leading to identity fraud for the victims.
**Financial loss**: ransom payments, repair costs, lost sales while systems are down.
**Fines** under data protection law for failing to protect data.
**Damage to reputation** and loss of customer trust.
**Downtime**: staff cannot work, lessons stop, appointments are cancelled.

explain.h: Why people are the weak point
p: Software can be updated and tested. People get tired, rushed and trusting. An attacker who sends 1,000 phishing emails needs only **one** person to click. This is why the exam links social engineering to **staff training** and **user access levels**: if the person who clicks has limited access, the damage is limited too.
Malware is bad software. It attacks the computer. Social engineering tricks a person. It attacks you, not the machine.

list: Virus: hides in a file. Runs when you open the file. Damages data.
Worm: copies itself across the network on its own. Slows everything down.
Trojan: looks like a useful program. You install it. It lets the attacker in.
Spyware: watches what you type and sends it to the attacker.
Ransomware: locks your files. Asks for money to unlock them.

simple.h: Three ways to trick a person
list: Phishing: a fake email or text. It asks you to log in or click a link.
Blagging: a made-up story. 'I am from IT. What is your password?'
Shouldering: someone watches you type your PIN.
Data is stolen.
Money is lost.
The company gets a fine.
People stop trusting it.
Work stops.

keyterms.def: Software written to damage, steal from or take control of a computer system.
Malware that attaches to a file and copies itself when the infected file is run.
Malware that copies itself across a network without any user action.
Malware disguised as legitimate software that the user installs willingly.
Malware that secretly records a user's activity, such as keystrokes, and sends it to an attacker.
Malware that encrypts a user's files and demands payment for the key to unlock them.
Manipulating people into giving away information or access rather than attacking the technology.
Fake messages or websites that pretend to be a trusted organisation to steal login details or install malware.

try.title: 1. Explore the threats
instructions: Work through the threats section. For each malware type, write one sentence: what it does AND how it spreads.
Find the social engineering examples. Which one would most likely work on you? Be honest, then say why.

try.title: 2. Name that attack
p: Read each scenario. Write the name of the attack and one clue that gave it away.
steps: A text says 'Your parcel could not be delivered. Pay £1.99 redelivery fee at this link.' The link goes to a site you have never heard of.
A school's network slows to a crawl. Every computer has a copy of the same program, which nobody installed.
A free 'video downloader' app works fine, but the attacker can now read files on your laptop.
A caller says 'Hi, it's Sam from the IT helpdesk. We are resetting accounts today. Can you confirm your current password?'
A pupil at the next desk watches your fingers as you type your login.
All the files on the office PCs now end in `.locked` and a message demands 0.5 bitcoin.
after: Answers: 1 phishing · 2 worm · 3 trojan · 4 blagging · 5 shouldering · 6 ransomware. Check your 'clue' matches the definition, not just a guess.

try.title: 3. Phishing clue checker
p: This program checks an email for common phishing clues. Run it, then add two more clue words or sender checks of your own. It is a teaching toy — real spam filters are far more complex — but it shows that phishing has a **pattern**.
try.code:
# Spot the phishing clues in a message (teaching toy only)
emails = [
    {"sender": "security@my-bank-login-help.com", "text": "URGENT: verify your account now or it will be closed"},
    {"sender": "office@school.sch.je", "text": "Reminder: parents evening is on Thursday"},
    {"sender": "prize@win-free-phone.biz", "text": "Congratulations! Click here to claim your free prize"},
]

clue_words = ["urgent", "verify", "click here", "prize", "closed", "password"]
trusted_domains = ["school.sch.je"]

for e in emails:
    score = 0
    reasons = []
    for word in clue_words:
        if word in e["text"].lower():
            score += 1
            reasons.append("word: " + word)
    domain = e["sender"].split("@")[1]
    if domain not in trusted_domains:
        score += 1
        reasons.append("unknown sender domain: " + domain)
    if "-" in domain:
        score += 1
        reasons.append("hyphenated look-alike domain")
    verdict = "SUSPICIOUS" if score >= 2 else "probably fine"
    print(e["sender"], "->", verdict, "(score", score, ")")
    for r in reasons:
        print("   ", r)
    print()

# TODO: add two more clue words and one more trusted domain, then rerun.

try.title: 4. Card sort: machine or person?
p: Cut out (or write) nine cards: virus, worm, trojan, spyware, ransomware, phishing, blagging, shouldering, 'leaving a password on a sticky note'. Sort them into two piles: **attacks the machine (malware)** and **attacks the person (social engineering / human error)**.
steps: Now sort the malware pile a second way: **needs a human to run it** vs **spreads by itself**.
Write one sentence for the sticky-note card: it is not an attack, so what is it? (A vulnerability that makes shouldering and blagging easier.)

try.title: 5. Key terms and impact ladder
instructions: Find the network security terms. Test yourself on the eight from today until you can give each definition without looking.
Then, on paper: a hospital is hit by ransomware. Write five consequences in order from 'happens first' to 'happens months later'. Use the words data, money, fine, trust, downtime at least once each.

check.q: Which type of malware spreads across a network WITHOUT a user doing anything?
check.fb: A worm self-replicates over network connections; a virus needs a host file to be run.

check.q: A free game installer secretly gives an attacker remote access. This is a:
check.fb: Disguised as useful software and installed by the user = trojan.

check.q: Which of these is social engineering?
opts: Phoning staff pretending to be IT to get a password
check.fb: Blagging manipulates a person; the other three are malware behaviours.

check.q: The main clue that an email is phishing is usually:
opts: It creates urgency and asks you to log in via a link
It is from a company you use
check.fb: Urgency plus a request for credentials via a link is the classic pattern.

check.q: Why are people described as the 'weak point' in network security?
opts: They forget to turn computers off
They can be tricked into giving access that software would refuse
check.fb: Social engineering bypasses technical defences by targeting trust and haste.

exam.q: Describe the difference between a **virus** and a **worm**.
model: A virus attaches itself to a file/program and needs a user to run it before it spreads (1), whereas a worm replicates itself across a network on its own without user action (1).
exam.commentary: The mark is in the contrast: *needs a host and a user* versus *self-replicating across a network*. 'A virus damages files and a worm spreads' is two separate facts, not a difference, and scores one at most.

exam.q: A member of staff receives a phone call from someone claiming to be from the company's bank, asking for the online banking password 'to fix a problem'. State the name of this type of attack and explain **one** way the company could reduce the risk of it succeeding.
model: Blagging / pretexting / social engineering (1). Train staff never to give out passwords by phone (1) because the bank/IT would never ask for them, so staff recognise the request as an attack (1). Or: have a policy to call back on a known official number (1) so the identity of the caller is checked before anything is shared (1).
exam.commentary: 'Phishing' for a phone call is a common slip — phishing is messages/websites; a spoken story is blagging. Credit 'social engineering' as the general term. The explain mark needs *because*: training works because staff then recognise and refuse the request.

exam.q: An online shop has suffered a ransomware attack. Explain **two** impacts this could have on the business.
model: Files/databases are encrypted so staff cannot access orders or stock (1), meaning the shop cannot trade and loses sales while systems are down (1). Customer personal/payment data may be stolen or lost (1), leading to a fine under data protection law and/or loss of customer trust and reputation (1). Also creditable: cost of paying the ransom or of restoring systems from backup (1) + consequence (1).
exam.commentary: Two impacts, each developed: what happens + what that means for the business. 'It loses money' twice counts once. The strongest answers tie the impact to *an online shop*: no website, no sales.

home: Find a real phishing message (your own, with personal details hidden, or a screenshot online). Annotate it with at least four clues that show it is fake. Then write the two-sentence warning you would send to a grandparent about it.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 5 · explain 12 · try 25 · check 5 · exam 10 · homework 3
misconceptions: 'Virus' used as the word for all malware. Insist on the five names; in the exam, 'virus' for a self-spreading network infection loses the mark.
Phishing used for every social engineering attack. Phishing = fake message/website. A phone story is blagging. Watching a screen is shouldering.
Thinking social engineering is a type of malware. It is the opposite: no software exploit, just a person being tricked.
Impact answers that stop at 'the company loses money'. Push for the chain: data lost -> fine -> reputation -> customers leave.
say: 'Virus needs you. Worm does not. Trojan is invited.'
'The attacker does not need to beat the firewall if they can beat the receptionist.'
'Phishing is written. Blagging is spoken. Shouldering is watched.'
teacher.skip: Try 5 can go; Try 2 and Try 4 carry the exam skill. Try 3 is optional if there is no Python time.
differentiation: Support: give the malware table with the 'how it spreads' column blank and the five phrases to match in.
Stretch: research one real ransomware incident on a public body (e.g. a health service or council) and present its impact chain in five bullet points, with no technical jargon.
